question: Which statement best describes Main idea?
options: A class gives CSS a reusable way to select one or more elements. For example, `.notice` can style several notice containers consistently. It is like giving related boxes the same label. Name a class by its purpose or role so the stylesheet remains understandable when colors and layout change. In a real page, use a nav element instead of a div when the group is site navigation.

A `div` does not become a button simply because CSS makes it look clickable. It lacks built-in keyboard behavior, focus, and button semantics. This is like painting a handle on a wall without installing a door. Use `<button>` for actions and `<a>` for navigation so browser behavior and assistive technology work correctly. In a real page, do not add a click handler to a div when a button fits the action.

`<div>` is a generic block container. It starts a new block in normal page flow and can group several elements. It is like an empty storage box with no label. Add a class when the group needs styling, but choose a semantic element when the group is navigation, an article, a header, or another named part. In a real page, use a div to group a card’s image, heading, and description for layout.

`<span>` is a generic inline container. It can wrap a short phrase inside a sentence without creating a new block. It is like highlighting a few words on a page. Use it when those words need a style or scripting hook, and avoid nesting spans just to create visual spacing. In a real page, wrap one word in a span only when that phrase needs a style or script hook.
explanation: `<div>` is a generic block container. It starts a new block in normal page flow and can group several elements. It is like an empty storage box with no label. Add a class when the group needs styling, but choose a semantic element when the group is navigation, an article, a header, or another named part. In a real page, use a div to group a card’s image, heading, and description for layout.
